A2.text:
Kamran is a student in Baku. He works in an office in summer and looks at a screen all day. In September, his uncle Vugar asked him to help on his farm in a rural village near Gakh. It was harvest time for hazelnuts.

“Farm work is easy,” Kamran thought.

He was wrong. They started at six in the morning. They picked hazelnuts from the ground for ten hours. Kamran's back hurt, and his hands were black from the soil.

This year was difficult for Uncle Vugar. There was a drought in summer, and the crop was small. “We must work fast,” he said. “The rain can come next week. We must make hay while the sun shines.”

Uncle Vugar also has livestock: ten cows and many chickens. He does not use chemicals. Everything on his farm is organic.

In the evening, they drank tea. Kamran asked, “Why is food so expensive in Baku?”

Uncle Vugar explained the supply chain. “I sell my hazelnuts to a man. He sells them to a company. The company sells them to a shop. Everybody takes money.”

Uncle Vugar is a very down to earth man. He smiled and said, “You worked hard today. You will sleep well. You reap what you sow.”

Kamran slept for ten hours.

B1.text:
Kamran had grown up in a ninth-floor flat in Baku and had never seen where his food actually came from. So when his uncle Vugar called in September and asked for help with the hazelnut harvest in his village near Gakh, Kamran agreed immediately. He imagined fresh air, long lunches and maybe some photos for Instagram.

The first morning destroyed that idea. They started at six. By nine, Kamran's back was aching from bending to collect nuts from the ground. By noon, his hands were black with soil. By six in the evening, he could barely lift his tea glass.

It was a hard year for Uncle Vugar. A long summer drought had damaged the crop, and the harvest was a third smaller than usual. The weather forecast said heavy rain would arrive the following week, so there was no time to rest. “We make hay while the sun shines,” his uncle said every morning.

Vugar also kept livestock, and he had never used a chemical spray in his life. “My grandfather didn't need poison, and neither do I,” he said. “Organic isn't a fashion here. It's just farming.”

One evening, on the veranda, Kamran asked a question that had been bothering him. “If you sell hazelnuts so cheaply, why do they cost so much in Baku?”

His uncle drew a line on a napkin. “Me. Then a buyer from the village. Then a factory. Then a distributor. Then the shop. That's the supply chain. Everyone along the line takes a piece, and the farmer gets the smallest one.”

Despite his hard life, Vugar was the most down to earth person Kamran knew. He never complained; he simply worked.

On the last day, with the harvest finally in and the first clouds arriving over the mountains, Vugar handed him a heavy bag of hazelnuts. “These are yours. You picked them.”

“I don't deserve all these,” Kamran laughed.

“You worked,” his uncle said. “You reap what you sow. That's the only rule out here.”

B2.text:
Kamran had spent his entire life on the ninth floor of a Baku apartment block and had only the haziest notion of where his food came from before it appeared in a supermarket. So when his uncle Vugar rang in September to ask for help with the hazelnut harvest in his village near Gakh, Kamran accepted on the spot, picturing mountain air, leisurely lunches and a few flattering photos for social media.

The first morning demolished the fantasy. Work began at six. By nine, his back was screaming from hours of stooping to gather nuts from the ground; by noon, his hands were caked in dark soil and his phone had given up searching for a signal; by evening, he could scarcely lift a glass of tea.

It was a punishing year for his uncle. A prolonged summer drought had stunted the crop, leaving the harvest a third smaller than usual, and the forecast promised heavy rain the following week. There was no question of rest. “We make hay while the sun shines,” Vugar announced each dawn, already lacing his boots.

He also kept livestock — a dozen cows, a small flock of sheep and an uncountable population of chickens — and had never sprayed a chemical on his land in his life. “My grandfather managed without poison, and so do I,” he shrugged. “Out here, organic isn't a marketing label. It's simply how farming is done.”

One evening on the veranda, Kamran voiced a question that had been nagging at him. “If you sell hazelnuts for so little, why do they cost a fortune in Baku?”

Vugar took a napkin and drew a line of dots. “Me. A village buyer. A processing plant. A distributor. The shop. That's your supply chain. Everyone along the way takes a slice, and the farmer — who did the work — gets the thinnest one.”

For all the hardship of rural life, Vugar remained the most down to earth man Kamran had ever met: no complaints, no speeches, only work.

On the final day, as the last sacks were loaded and the first dark clouds rolled over the peaks, Vugar handed him a heavy bag of hazelnuts. “Yours. You picked them.”

“I hardly deserve this many,” Kamran protested.

“You worked,” his uncle said simply. “You reap what you sow. That's the only law up here.”

podcast.title: Three tiny tomatoes

before.predict: Do you know where your food comes from? Guess: where did Sam spend last weekend?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is farming and where our food comes from. And I spent last weekend on a farm!
At my uncle's place in Guba?
Yes! The apple harvest. Two days of picking apples from morning to evening.
Guba apples are famous. Were you tired?
My arms hurt more than my legs after a race. But the apples were amazing.
My uncle says it was a good year. Last year there was a drought — no rain for two months.
What happened to the crop?
They lost almost half of it. Farmers are always fighting the weather.
Your uncle doesn't use chemicals, does he?
No, everything is organic. He says good soil is the most important thing on a farm.
He's so calm and kind. Very down to earth.
That's rural life. Early to bed, early to rise. No traffic, no deadlines.
Except the weather. On Saturday it looked like rain, so we worked until dark.
Make hay while the sun shines, as they say.
Exactly. And now I'm trying to grow tomatoes on my balcony.
How's it going?
Three tomatoes in two months. [laugh] Very small ones.
Well, you reap what you sow. Maybe give them more water and sun.
And more love. I talk to them every morning.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: do you know where your food comes from — and could you live on a farm?
I could. For two days. See you next time!
Bye for now!
